messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eliyah, a 21‑year‑old forester of Middle Eastern descent, recalls the night the highway crash unfolded before her. The scene was a tableau of splintered metal, blood smeared on the gravel, and the acrid smell of burning tires that still clung to her memory. Whenever she drives a work truck or hears a co‑worker discuss a recent accident, the sight of blood, the talk about crashes, and the images of cars colliding flood her senses. The intensity of these triggers is enough to push her into the maladaptive routine she has since adopted: she stays awake until the early hours of the morning, scanning the sky for signs of danger, and avoids any conversation that might remind her of the event. The same triggers that force her into late nights and hyper‑vigilance also bring her memories rushing forward. A whiff of diesel, a distant crash, or a casual remark about a car crash will suddenly set her mind back to the highway. In those moments, the smell of blood, the echo of splintered metal, and the visual detail of twisted bodies return with a scent that makes her chest tighten. Her memories feel alien, as if they belong to a stranger rather than to her own experience, and she pushes them away before she can fully recall them. The triggers do more than summon memories; they remind her of the personal failure she feels she endured. Each time she sees blood or hears people talk about a crash, she is flooded with the thought that she had failed to protect the drivers, that her own values were violated, and that she had lost her former happiness. The emotional sting of these recollections turns her internal narrative into a harsh self‑judgment, solidifying a negative appraisal of herself and her actions. The harsh self‑judgment feeds into the same maladaptive behaviors that were initially triggered by the event. Eliyah’s sense that she has violated her own values and failed to protect others makes her dread any potential reminders. She avoids conversations about crashes, resists answering calls from colleagues who might mention the incident, and postpones sleep because staying up seems the only way to keep her thoughts in check. Her avoidance becomes a self‑fulfilling defense against the distressing appraisal she feels toward herself. In turn, that negative appraisal makes her memory of the event even more fragmentary. The shame she feels about not intervening pushes her to block out the details before they can be fully recalled, reinforcing the alien quality of the memory. The more she pushes the memory away, the more she believes she has lost her sense of agency and identity, deepening her sense of failure. The alien and odor‑laden memory of the crash keeps Eliyah’s maladaptive coping in place. When she recalls the smell of blood and the disjointed images of twisted bodies, her body reacts by staying awake, by checking her surroundings for any sign of danger, and by avoiding any reminders. The intensity of the memory’s sensory cues serves as a constant reminder that the threat is still present, and thus her maladaptive strategies persist. The memory also strengthens her negative appraisal by feeding her a sense of helplessness. Each recall of the event reinforces the idea that she could have prevented it and that she failed, thereby tightening the loop between memory and self‑criticism. Eliyah’s persistent avoidance and hyper‑vigilance, in turn, amplify the presence of triggers. By staying awake until the late hours, she is exposed to more of the late‑night radio chatter and late‑night traffic sounds that echo the crash. Her constant scanning of the forest for potential danger makes her more attuned to blood‑stained leaves and the rustling of a vehicle passing by. Her heightened awareness makes her more likely to encounter the very cues that once triggered her distress. Maladaptive strategies that keep her awake also heighten her sense of threat, making the triggers appear more imminent and terrifying. Each night she finds herself staring at the ceiling, listening to the faint hum of her truck’s engine, waiting for the slightest sign that a crash might be imminent, even when nothing is happening. This cycle of vigilance, memory recall, and negative self‑appraisal has now become so entrenched that she feels isolated, restless, and unable to return to the simple joy she once found in her forest work. It is this relentless cycle that finally brings Eliyah to the clinic. After a week of missing work, her supervisor noticed her eyes were sunken and her voice barely hushed. Eliyah confided that the night she saw the crash and the days that followed left her feeling “broken,” that she no longer could enjoy the trees she had always loved. Her greatest fear is that she will never be able to protect those around her again, while her hope is that she can regain the sense of purpose she lost. The moment she decided to seek help, she realized that the only way to break free was to address the interconnected web of triggers, memories, negative appraisals, and maladaptive coping that kept her locked in its own relentless loop.
